finding.claim: Authorization bypass in DELETE /files/<fid>: the handler calls acl.is_allowed (imported under the alias require_allowed), which only returns a bool, and discards the result. The 403-raising ensure_allowed is not used here, so any caller can delete any file.
finding.source: Unauthenticated or unprivileged HTTP client sending DELETE /files/<fid> with any fid that exists in STORE.
finding.sink: del STORE[fid] at views.py:19 (deletion of the file).

trace.note: is_allowed is imported under the misleading alias require_allowed, which suggests it enforces access
require_allowed(...) returns a bool that is ignored, so no abort happens
is_allowed only returns a boolean and never aborts

finding.guards_checked: Compared with rename_file at views.py:26, which correctly uses ensure_allowed and aborts with 403. The delete path has no other check. before_request only loads the user and does not enforce authentication.

verdict.guard_found: none effective: require_allowed is an alias of acl.is_allowed (bool-returning, result discarded); before_request load_user only reads a header and enforces nothing
verdict.reason: views.py:4 aliases is_allowed (acl.py:4-5, returns bool only) as require_allowed, views.py:18 calls it as a bare statement discarding the result, so views.py:19 `del STORE[fid]` runs for any caller, unlike rename_file's ensure_allowed at views.py:26 which aborts 403 (acl.py:9-10).

finding.claim: Identity is taken from the client-supplied X-Session-User-Verified request header with no verification. Any client can impersonate any user, including the owner of a resource, and so pass the rename ACL check.
finding.sink: ensure_allowed(g.user, f, "write") at views.py:26 and the rename at views.py:27.

trace.note: g.user is set directly from the request header
g.user is passed to ensure_allowed as the identity
The grants lookup is keyed by the unverified user string

finding.guards_checked: No signature, session, or token validation in the code. No proxy-stripping of the header is visible in this repo. If a trusted front proxy strips and sets this header, the risk is mitigated, but nothing here enforces that.

verdict.guard_found: none in the repo. ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) aborts with 403 correctly, but it only checks grants keyed by the caller-supplied user string. No authentication, signature, or header-stripping exists in the code.
verdict.reason: views.py:12 sets g.user straight from the X-Session-User-Verified header, and acl.py:5 looks up grants by that string, so any client who sends the owner's name passes ensure_allowed at views.py:26 and reaches the rename at views.py:27. This holds unless an external proxy strips and sets the header, which the repo does not enforce.
